sections.title: What is JPA?
sections.content:
Java Persistence API (JPA) is a specification — not an implementation. It defines a standard way for Java applications to interact with relational databases using an object-oriented paradigm, mapping Java classes (entities) to database tables and Java objects to rows. Because it is a specification, you choose an implementation: Hibernate is by far the most popular, with EclipseLink and OpenJPA also available. Spring Boot auto-configures Hibernate as the JPA provider.

The central JPA abstraction is the EntityManager. It is your gateway to the persistence context — a first-level cache and change tracker that keeps track of all managed entities within a transaction. When you call entityManager.find(), persist(), merge(), or remove(), you are working through the EntityManager. In Spring Data JPA, you rarely use EntityManager directly; the JpaRepository interface wraps it. But understanding it is critical for grasping what happens behind the scenes.

The persistence context has a lifecycle tied to a unit of work (usually a transaction). Within a transaction, every entity you load or persist is 'managed' — Hibernate watches it for changes. At the end of the transaction (flush time), Hibernate compares every managed entity to its snapshot taken when it was loaded (dirty checking) and issues UPDATE SQL for any that changed. This automatic dirty checking is one of JPA's most powerful features and a common source of confusion — you do not need to call save() to persist changes to a managed entity.

Understanding JPA as a spec versus Hibernate as an implementation matters because some features (like batch inserts, @BatchSize, @Filter) are Hibernate-specific extensions. Portability across JPA providers is a theoretical goal; in practice most Spring Boot apps are tightly coupled to Hibernate.

sections.title: Entity Mapping
sections.content:
An entity is a Java class mapped to a database table. It must be annotated with @Entity (marks it as a JPA entity) and must have a no-argument constructor (required by JPA to instantiate objects when loading from the database). The class name maps to a table with the same name by default; use @Table(name = "custom_name") to override this.

Every entity must have a primary key field annotated with @Id. The field type can be Long, Integer, UUID, or String. Without a primary key, JPA cannot identify rows and Hibernate will throw an exception at startup. The @GeneratedValue annotation tells JPA to auto-generate the key — the strategy you choose determines how.

Field-level mapping is done with @Column. Without @Column, JPA maps each field to a column with the same name (converted to snake_case by Spring Boot's default naming strategy). @Column lets you specify the exact column name, nullable constraint, length, unique constraint, and whether the column is insertable/updatable. Primitive types (int, long) are always NOT NULL; wrapper types (Integer, Long) can be null.

Transient fields — those you do not want persisted — get @Transient. This is common for computed fields or fields used for business logic that should not touch the database. The @Basic annotation is implied on all persistable fields; you only need it explicitly if you want to change fetch type (FetchType.LAZY for a blob field, for example).

sections.title: Primary Key Strategies
sections.content:
Choosing the right primary key generation strategy affects performance, portability, and the ability to know the ID before inserting. JPA provides four strategies via @GeneratedValue(strategy = ...).

GenerationType.IDENTITY relies on the database's auto-increment column (MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT, PostgreSQL's SERIAL/BIGSERIAL). The ID is generated by the database when the row is inserted. The downside: Hibernate cannot batch INSERT statements with IDENTITY strategy because it needs to execute each insert individually to retrieve the generated key via getGeneratedKeys().

GenerationType.SEQUENCE uses a database sequence object. Hibernate calls nextval('sequence_name') to obtain the next ID before the INSERT, allowing it to know the ID upfront and batch multiple inserts. Sequences are more efficient and are the recommended strategy for PostgreSQL. Configure them with @SequenceGenerator to control the sequence name and allocationSize (how many IDs to pre-allocate per round trip — default 50, reducing DB calls).

GenerationType.AUTO lets JPA choose based on the database dialect. With Hibernate 5+, AUTO on MySQL maps to TABLE strategy (very slow); on PostgreSQL it maps to SEQUENCE. Avoid AUTO — be explicit.

For UUID primary keys, use @GeneratedValue(generator = "UUID") with @GenericGenerator(name = "UUID", strategy = "org.hibernate.id.UUIDGenerator"), or in Hibernate 6 simply annotate a UUID field with @UuidGenerator. UUIDs make IDs globally unique (good for distributed systems) but are larger and less index-friendly than Long.

sections.title: Basic Types and Converters
sections.content:
JPA supports mapping standard Java types to database columns automatically: String to VARCHAR, Integer/Long to INT/BIGINT, Boolean to BOOLEAN or TINYINT(1), Date/LocalDate/LocalDateTime to DATE/DATETIME, and byte[] to BLOB. For enums, BigDecimal, and other types, explicit configuration is often needed.

For enum fields, use @Enumerated. @Enumerated(EnumType.ORDINAL) stores the enum's ordinal position (0, 1, 2...) — compact but fragile: reordering enum constants breaks existing data. @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) stores the enum name as a string — less compact but safe. Always prefer STRING in production code.

For legacy date types, @Temporal specifies whether a java.util.Date field maps to DATE (date only), TIME (time only), or TIMESTAMP. With Java 8+ types (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime), @Temporal is not needed — JPA 2.2 and Hibernate 5 handle these natively.

AttributeConverter lets you map a custom Java type to a database column type. Implement AttributeConverter<JavaType, DbType>, annotate with @Converter(autoApply = true) to apply globally, or use @Convert(converter = MyConverter.class) on individual fields. Common uses: encrypting sensitive fields before storage, storing a JSON object as a TEXT column, mapping a custom value object. This is a clean extension point that keeps mapping logic out of your entity.

sections.title: @OneToOne
sections.content:
A @OneToOne relationship maps a one-to-one association between two entities. A classic example is a User and a UserProfile — each user has exactly one profile. The mapping can be unidirectional (only one side has the annotation) or bidirectional (both sides reference each other).

In a unidirectional @OneToOne, you place the annotation on the owning entity's field and use @JoinColumn to specify the foreign key column. The owning side is the table that holds the foreign key. In a bidirectional mapping, the non-owning side uses mappedBy to refer to the field on the owning side — this tells JPA it doesn't manage the foreign key; it just reads it through the owning side.

OrphanRemoval = true means when you remove a UserProfile from a User, the profile entity is automatically deleted from the database. Without it, removing the reference just nulls the foreign key column (or causes a constraint violation). Use orphanRemoval carefully — it's powerful but can cause unexpected cascading deletes if you're not aware of it.

For a performance optimization, @OneToOne can use a shared primary key strategy with @PrimaryKeyJoinColumn. Instead of a separate foreign key column, the child entity's ID equals the parent's ID. This saves a column and a join but requires more careful management. @OneToOne is EAGER by default — consider making it LAZY if you don't always need the associated entity, to avoid N+1 issues with collections of entities.

sections.title: @OneToMany and @ManyToOne
sections.content:
One-to-many is the most common relationship in domain models: one Order has many OrderItems, one Department has many Employees. In JPA, this relationship is expressed with @OneToMany on the 'one' side and @ManyToOne on the 'many' side. For bidirectional mappings, understanding the 'owning side' concept is critical — the owning side is the one that controls the foreign key column in the database.

In a bidirectional @OneToMany / @ManyToOne: the @ManyToOne side is ALWAYS the owning side (it holds the foreign key column). The @OneToMany side uses mappedBy to point to the field on the @ManyToOne side. This means when you add an item to order.getItems(), if you don't also set item.setOrder(order), Hibernate won't persist the relationship correctly because the owning side didn't change. Always update both sides of a bidirectional relationship, or use a helper method.

CascadeType controls which operations on the parent propagate to children. CascadeType.PERSIST means saving a parent also saves unsaved children. CascadeType.MERGE syncs detached children. CascadeType.REMOVE deletes children when the parent is deleted. CascadeType.ALL includes everything. Use CascadeType.ALL cautiously — it includes REMOVE, which can cause mass deletes. A safer default for most relationships is CascadeType.PERSIST, CascadeType.MERGE.

The @JoinColumn annotation on the @ManyToOne side specifies the foreign key column name. Without it, JPA generates a default name (field name + _ + referenced column name). Always specify explicit column names for clarity and database schema control.

sections.title: @ManyToMany
sections.content:
A many-to-many relationship requires a join table: a Student can enroll in many Courses, and each Course has many Students. JPA manages this join table automatically with @ManyToMany and @JoinTable. The @JoinTable annotation on the owning side specifies the join table name and the foreign key columns on both sides.

The owning side of @ManyToMany carries the @JoinTable annotation. The inverse side uses mappedBy. Only the owning side is responsible for synchronizing the join table — changes made only to the inverse side's collection won't be persisted. As with @OneToMany, always update both sides when working with bidirectional @ManyToMany.

Avoid infinite recursion in JSON serialization: if Student has a List<Course> and Course has a List<Student>, Jackson will follow references indefinitely and overflow the stack. Solutions: @JsonIgnore on one side, @JsonManagedReference/@JsonBackReference, using DTO projections (recommended for APIs), or @JsonIdentityInfo.

In practice, explicit join entity classes (sometimes called 'association entities') are often preferable to pure @ManyToMany. If the join table has additional columns (enrollment date, grade), you must use a join entity. Even without extra columns, explicit entities give you more control over cascading, fetching, and querying. Model it as @ManyToOne from both sides to the join entity instead.

sections.title: Cascade and Orphan Removal
sections.content:
Cascade types determine which persistence operations on a parent entity are automatically applied to its associated child entities. Getting cascades wrong is a common source of bugs — either operations don't propagate when expected, or they propagate too aggressively.

CascadeType.PERSIST: when you persist a parent, associated new children are also persisted. This is essential when creating a parent with children in one operation (e.g., new Order with OrderItems). Without PERSIST, you'd have to manually persist each child. CascadeType.MERGE: when you merge a detached parent, its children are also merged. Important for update operations with detached entities. CascadeType.REMOVE: when you remove a parent, all children are also removed. Use carefully — deleting an Order would delete all its OrderItems. For some relationships (like a Product that has Orders) this would be disastrous.

CascadeType.DETACH, REFRESH, and REPLICATE are less commonly used but follow the same pattern: the operation is cascaded to associated entities. CascadeType.ALL is shorthand for all types.

OrphanRemoval = true on @OneToMany or @OneToOne means: if a child entity is removed from the parent's collection (or the reference is set to null), it is automatically deleted from the database. This is independent of cascade — you don't need CascadeType.REMOVE to use orphanRemoval. The key semantic difference: orphanRemoval handles the case where you remove an item from a collection; CascadeType.REMOVE handles the case where you delete the parent. For 'owned' child entities that have no meaning without their parent (like OrderItems without an Order), use both orphanRemoval = true and CascadeType.ALL.

sections.title: EAGER vs LAZY Loading
sections.content:
Fetching strategy controls when associated entities are loaded from the database: immediately (EAGER) or on first access (LAZY). Choosing correctly has major performance implications.

FetchType.EAGER means: when you load the parent entity, Hibernate immediately loads the association too — either via a JOIN in the same query or a separate SELECT. EAGER is the default for @ManyToOne and @OneToOne. The reasoning is that these are single entities, not collections, so the overhead is bounded.

FetchType.LAZY means: the association is represented by a proxy object. No database query is issued when the parent is loaded. The query fires only when you actually access the collection or object — for example, calling order.getItems().size(). LAZY is the default for @OneToMany and @ManyToMany. The problem: if the persistence context is closed when you access the proxy (e.g., outside a @Transactional method), you get a LazyInitializationException.

The default EAGER for @ManyToOne can cause the N+1 problem: loading 100 Orders each with an EAGER Customer triggers 100 + 1 queries (1 for orders, 100 for customers). The counterintuitive rule: always default to LAZY for everything, and use explicit JOIN FETCH queries or @EntityGraph when you need associated data. EAGER is rarely the right choice in production code because it removes your ability to control when data is loaded.

sections.title: N+1 Problem
sections.content:
The N+1 problem is one of the most common and costly JPA performance issues. It occurs when your code loads N parent entities and then accesses a LAZY-loaded association on each one, triggering N additional SELECT queries — 1 query for the parents plus N queries for the children.

A concrete example: you load a list of 100 Orders. If Order has a LAZY @ManyToOne Customer, and your code calls order.getCustomer().getName() for each order, Hibernate fires 1 query to load all orders, then 100 separate queries to load each customer: 101 queries total. With EAGER, it would fire 100 SELECTs for customers when loading orders. Either way it's bad. The solution is to load what you need in a single query using JOIN FETCH.

JOIN FETCH in JPQL tells Hibernate to include the associated entity in the same SELECT: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer. This generates a SQL JOIN and populates the customer association with no additional queries. Even if customer is marked LAZY, JOIN FETCH overrides it for this specific query. Similarly for collections: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items loads orders with their items in one query (with a caveat: join-fetching a collection causes duplicate parent rows that must be handled with DISTINCT).

Hibernate provides the hibernate.show_sql and hibernate.format_sql properties for logging queries. Always enable SQL logging in development and audit the number of queries per request. If you see repetitive queries for the same entity type, you likely have an N+1 problem. Tools like p6spy, datasource-proxy, or Hypersistence Optimizer can automatically detect N+1 issues.

sections.title: Entity Graph
sections.content:
Entity graphs provide a declarative, reusable way to specify which associations to fetch eagerly for a specific query, without writing JPQL JOIN FETCH clauses. They are ideal when you have many repository methods that need the same association loaded, or when you want to change fetching behavior without modifying JPQL.

Define a named entity graph on the entity class with @NamedEntityGraph. The attributePaths list the association field names to include. For nested associations, use @NamedSubgraph. Apply the graph to a Spring Data repository method using @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {...}) or referencing the named graph.

There are two types of entity graphs: FETCH (specified paths are EAGER, unspecified are LAZY) and LOAD (specified paths are EAGER, unspecified follow their default fetch types). FETCH is usually what you want — load exactly what you specify, lazy-load everything else.

Entity graphs work well for simple to moderately complex cases. For very deep association trees or complex conditional fetching (load items only if the order is in PROCESSING status), custom JPQL with JOIN FETCH offers more control. The combination — default LAZY on all associations, targeted JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph per query — is the recommended production pattern.

sections.title: Second-Level Cache
sections.content:
JPA's first-level cache is the persistence context itself — it caches entities within a single transaction/session. If you load Order with ID 1 twice in the same transaction, only one database query fires. But this cache is discarded when the transaction ends.

The second-level cache (L2C) lives at the EntityManagerFactory level, shared across all transactions and sessions. If Order 1 is in the L2C, any request can load it without hitting the database. Hibernate supports pluggable L2C providers: Ehcache, Caffeine (via Hibernate-jcache), Infinispan, and Hazelcast are common choices.

Enable the L2C per entity with @Cache on the entity class. The CacheConcurrencyStrategy determines read/write behavior: READ_ONLY for entities that never change (reference data like countries, currencies); NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE for entities that are occasionally updated (eventual consistency); READ_WRITE for entities needing strict consistency (more locking overhead); TRANSACTIONAL for full transactional isolation (JTA required).

Collections can also be cached with @Cache on the collection field. The query cache is a separate feature that caches the IDs returned by JPQL queries — useful for queries with stable results. Cache invalidation is automatic for entities Hibernate manages (UPDATE/DELETE clears the cached entry), but direct JDBC or native SQL updates bypass the cache and cause stale reads. The L2C is most beneficial for read-heavy, rarely-changing reference data; it adds complexity and can cause stale data bugs if misused.

sections.title: JPQL
sections.content:
JPQL (Java Persistence Query Language) is an object-oriented query language that operates on entity objects and their fields — not tables and columns. This abstraction means your queries are portable across databases (the JPA provider translates JPQL to the appropriate SQL dialect) and refactor-safe when your entity names change (though IDE support for JPQL refactoring is limited).

JPQL syntax resembles SQL but uses entity class names and field names: SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email. The FROM clause references the entity class name (case-sensitive), not the table name. Aliases (u) are mandatory. Named parameters (:email) are preferred over positional parameters (?1) for readability. Named queries can be defined on the entity with @NamedQuery and referenced by name for performance (they can be pre-compiled at startup).

JPQL supports JOIN for navigating associations: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN o.customer c WHERE c.city = 'London'. Note this is an INNER JOIN — only orders with a customer are returned. Use LEFT JOIN to include orders without customers. JOIN FETCH (discussed in the N+1 section) eagerly loads the association. You can join across multiple relationships: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN o.items i JOIN i.product p WHERE p.category = :cat.

Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX), GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, and DISTINCT all work in JPQL as expected. JPQL does not support INSERT or full DDL — use native queries for those. For projections (loading only specific columns rather than full entities), see the Spring Data @Query section.

sections.title: Criteria API
sections.content:
The Criteria API provides a type-safe, programmatic way to build JPQL queries in Java code. Instead of string queries, you use Java objects: CriteriaBuilder for constructing expressions, CriteriaQuery for defining what to select, Root for the entity being queried, and Predicate for WHERE conditions.

The primary advantage over JPQL strings is compile-time safety: if you rename an entity field, the Criteria API code fails to compile (assuming you use metamodel classes). The downside is verbosity — a simple 3-line JPQL query becomes 10+ lines of Criteria API code. The Criteria API shines for dynamic queries where the number and combination of WHERE conditions depends on runtime values (e.g., a search form with optional filters).

JPA generates metamodel classes (e.g., User_) from your entities that provide type-safe field references like User_.email. Configure the hibernate-jpamodelgen annotation processor to generate these automatically. Without the metamodel, you use string-based field names: root.get("email"), losing type safety.

Spring Data's Specifications (JpaSpecificationExecutor) wrap the Criteria API in a composable pattern. A Specification<T> is a single Predicate factory. You compose multiple specifications with .and() and .or(), building complex queries from small, testable pieces without writing a custom Criteria API query for every combination.

sections.title: Spring Data Derived Queries
sections.content:
Spring Data JPA's killer feature is automatic query derivation from method names. You declare a method in your repository interface following a naming convention, and Spring Data parses the method name and generates the JPQL automatically — no @Query needed.

The method name consists of a subject keyword (find...By, count...By, exists...By, delete...By) followed by a predicate derived from entity field names and keywords. findByEmail finds by the email field. findByFirstNameAndLastName creates a query with two AND conditions. findByAgeGreaterThan generates a > comparison. findByNameContainingIgnoreCase generates a LIKE %name% with case insensitive comparison.

Keywords for comparisons: Equals (default), LessThan, LessThanEqual, GreaterThan, GreaterThanEqual, Between, Like, Containing (wrapped in %), StartingWith, EndingWith, In (accepts a Collection), NotNull, IsNull, True, False. Ordering: findTop3ByOrderBySalaryDesc selects 3 records ordered by salary descending. Count: findCountByDepartment.

Derived queries are elegant for simple conditions, but become unreadable for complex multi-field searches. The rule of thumb: if the method name is longer than about 60 characters, switch to @Query. Also, derived queries load full entity objects — use interface projections or DTO projections (@Query with constructor expression) when you only need a subset of fields.

sections.title: Spring Data @Query
sections.content:
When derived query methods become too complex or unreadable, @Query lets you write explicit JPQL (or native SQL) directly on the repository method. This gives full JPQL power — JOINs, subqueries, aggregations, DTO constructors — while keeping everything in the repository interface.

By default @Query uses JPQL. Set nativeQuery = true for native SQL, which is useful for database-specific syntax, bulk operations, or queries that are too complex for JPQL. Native queries bypass JPA's object mapping — results come back as Object[] or can be mapped to interface-based projections.

For UPDATE and DELETE operations, add @Modifying alongside @Query. Without @Modifying, Spring Data throws an exception because it expects queries to return entities. Also add @Transactional on the method (or on the calling service) because mutation requires a transaction. @Modifying also has a clearAutomatically = true option that clears the persistence context after execution, preventing stale entities from being returned by subsequent finds.

Projections are a powerful feature: instead of returning full entities, return only the fields you need. Interface-based projections declare an interface with getter methods matching field names — Spring Data auto-generates the implementation. DTO projections use a JPQL constructor expression: SELECT new com.app.dto.ProductSummaryDto(p.id, p.name, p.price) FROM Product p. Interface projections are more flexible (support nested projections) while DTO projections offer better performance by not loading entity proxy objects.

sections.title: @Transactional
sections.content:
@Transactional is Spring's declarative transaction management annotation. When applied to a method (or class), Spring wraps the method in a transaction proxy: a transaction is started before the method, and committed (or rolled back on exception) after. This eliminates manual connection.commit() / connection.rollback() boilerplate.

Propagation controls what happens when a @Transactional method is called within an existing transaction. REQUIRED (default): join the existing transaction or create a new one. This means if serviceA calls serviceB, and both are @Transactional(REQUIRED), they share one transaction — a failure in serviceB rolls back serviceA's changes too. REQUIRES_NEW: always suspend any existing transaction and create a new independent one. Useful for audit logging that must commit even if the main transaction fails. NESTED: creates a savepoint within the existing transaction; if the nested method fails, it rolls back to the savepoint without affecting the outer transaction.

Isolation levels control visibility of uncommitted data between concurrent transactions: READ_UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads possible — never use), READ_COMMITTED (default in most DBs, no dirty reads), REPEATABLE_READ (phantom reads possible but same row reads are consistent), SERIALIZABLE (fully isolated, no anomalies, slowest).

rollbackFor defines which exceptions trigger rollback. By default, Spring only rolls back on RuntimeException and Error — checked exceptions (IOException, etc.) do NOT trigger rollback unless listed in rollbackFor. readOnly = true is a performance hint: Hibernate skips dirty checking at flush time (since we won't write), and some databases use read-only transactions for additional optimizations like read replicas.

sections.title: Open Session in View Anti-pattern
sections.content:
LazyInitializationException is one of the most common JPA errors in Spring Boot applications. It happens when you try to access a LAZY-loaded association after the persistence context (session) is closed. The typical scenario: a @Service method loads an entity (within a @Transactional block), returns it to a @RestController, and the controller tries to serialize it to JSON — but the @Transactional has already ended, closing the session. Calling order.getItems() at that point fires the exception.

Spring Boot's 'Open Session in View' (OSIV) pattern is enabled by default (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true). It keeps the Hibernate session open for the entire HTTP request lifecycle — from filter through controller through view. This 'fixes' LazyInitializationException silently: LAZY associations can be accessed anywhere in the request because the session never closes until the response is written. It sounds convenient, but it's widely considered an anti-pattern.

OSIV's problems: it causes silent N+1 issues in controllers and views where developers don't realize they're triggering database queries. It ties your database connection to the HTTP request duration, wasting connection pool resources. It blurs the line between the service and presentation layers. It generates queries at unpredictable times, making performance hard to analyze.

The correct solution: disable OSIV with spring.jpa.open-in-view=false and always return DTOs (not entities) from your service methods. Load all needed data within the @Transactional service method (using JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph), map to DTOs, and return the DTOs. No lazy loading needed outside the transaction, no lazy exceptions, predictable queries.

sections.title: Pagination and Sorting
sections.content:
Returning full tables to the client is impractical for large datasets. Spring Data JPA integrates Pageable and Sort to add pagination and sorting without manual LIMIT/OFFSET clauses.

The Pageable interface represents a page request: which page number (0-based), how many items per page, and an optional Sort. PageRequest.of(0, 20) requests the first page with 20 items. PageRequest.of(1, 20, Sort.by("createdAt").descending()) requests the second page sorted by createdAt descending. Pass Pageable directly to any repository method — Spring Data adds LIMIT/OFFSET to the generated SQL.

Repository methods return either Page<T> or Slice<T>. Page<T> includes the total number of elements and pages (fires an extra COUNT query). Slice<T> only knows if there's a next page (no COUNT query) — more efficient for infinite-scroll UIs where you don't need a total count. For very large tables, COUNT queries can be expensive; consider Slice<T> or query-count optimization with a simpler countQuery.

In @RestController you can declare Pageable as a method parameter directly — Spring MVC auto-binds from request parameters (page=0&size=20&sort=name,asc). Use @PageableDefault to provide defaults. Always expose DTO-based paged responses to clients, not raw Page<Entity>. The standard wrapper pattern is to map Page<Entity> to Page<Dto> using page.map(entity -> toDto(entity)).

sections.title: Auditing
sections.content:
Auditing — automatically tracking who created or last modified an entity and when — is a cross-cutting concern that should not require manual setCreatedAt() calls in every service method. Spring Data JPA's auditing infrastructure handles this declaratively with annotations.

Enable JPA auditing by adding @EnableJpaAuditing to a configuration class (or your main application class). Then annotate your entity fields: @CreatedDate populates the creation timestamp on first persist; @LastModifiedDate updates on every modification; @CreatedBy and @LastModifiedBy populate with the current user's identifier. Make your entity class extend or include an abstract auditable base class to avoid duplicating these fields.

For @CreatedBy and @LastModifiedBy to work, implement the AuditorAware<T> interface and define it as a bean. AuditorAware has one method: getCurrentAuditor() which returns an Optional of the auditor identifier. Typically this reads the username from the SecurityContextHolder. Register the bean name in @EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditorProvider").

The @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class) annotation on the entity class connects it to the auditing infrastructure. Spring Data also supports @Version for optimistic locking: a version field (@Version on Long or int) is auto-incremented on every update. If two concurrent transactions update the same entity, the second commit detects the version mismatch and throws OptimisticLockingFailureException, preventing lost updates without database-level locking.
